messages.subject: Interaction terms in lme
parts:
Hi R-learners, 

I’m not sure if this is a coding issue or a mis-understanding of the underlying statistics on my part, but I’m hoping someone can at least point me in the right direction. 

I’m modeling density of seedlings after a fire, with data taken over three years, using the lme() function from the nlme package. Replicates are at the plot level, with average seedling density “count.”  I’ve included “plot.code” as a random effect because each plot was sampled three times (“postfire.year”) and I don’t want to pseudo-replicate. 

I’m interested in both the effects of soil type (“soil”, a discrete variable which is either “S” for serpentine soils or “N” for non-serpentine soils) and within-type soil characteristics (“pc.1” and “pc.2” which are continuous PCA scores from a variety of other soil data). For simplicity’s sake I’m just going to talk about “pc.1” but the same issues apply to “pc.2”as well. 

A sample of the dataframe looks like this:
   plot.code       soil     pc.1      pc.2          count    postfire.year
1 N_LC_17_B    N 1.862677 1.2217352   3.2             1
2 N_LC_17_B    N 2.340146 0.4892991   3.2             1
3 N_LC_17_B    N 1.862677 1.2217352   0.4             2
4 N_LC_17_B    N 2.340146 0.4892991   0.4             2
5 N_LC_17_B    N 1.862677 1.2217352   1.4             3
6 N_LC_17_B    N 2.340146 0.4892991   1.4             3

I care more about the differences between soil types than the PCA scores, and I’m only interested in the within-soil-type effects of the PCA scores. 

When I set up my model with a full cross between soil type (“soil”), the differences between soil types get obscured by pc.1 because pc.1 is related to soil type. However, the returned fixed effect structure is as I expect (main soil type term, main pc.1 term, and the interaction term)

summary(lme(count ~ soil*pc.1, 
            random= ~1|plot.code, 
            data=filter(seed.dens.obligate)))

Fixed effects: count ~ soil + pc.1 * soil 
                 Value Std.Error  DF    t-value p-value
(Intercept)  1.9013061 2.0324224 329  0.9354877  0.3502
soilS        2.2164100 2.3048897  65  0.9616122  0.3398
pc.1        -0.1470138 0.9833641 329 -0.1495009  0.8812
soilS:pc.1   0.2734306 1.1453799 329  0.2387248  0.8115


What I’d like to do is run a model with just a main effect for soil, and then the interaction between soil type and pc.1 But when I do this, there are now two interaction terms in the model output, one for each soil type. 

summary(lme(count ~ soil + pc.1:soil, 
            random= ~1|plot.code, 
            data=filter(seed.dens.obligate)))

Fixed effects: count ~ soil + pc.1:soil 
                 Value Std.Error  DF    t-value p-value
(Intercept)  1.9013061 2.0324224 329  0.9354877  0.3502
soilS        2.2164100 2.3048897  65  0.9616122  0.3398
soilN:pc.1  -0.1470138 0.9833641 329 -0.1495009  0.8812
soilS:pc.1   0.1264168 0.5872735 329  0.2152605  0.8297

I haven’t had this issue when setting up a similar model formula using lm() when only taking one year of data (without the random effect). Any ideas for 1. Why I’m getting two interaction terms 2. If there’s a better way to do this? 

I’ve attached a simplified dataset. 

Thanks in advance,
Chhaya

~
Chhaya M. Werner

University of California Davis

parts:
Thank you for the explanation, that helps a lot! I was definitely over-thinking it. 

On Oct 3, 2018, at 4:42 PM, Evan Eskew <eve...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Chhaya,

I don't have time for a more in-depth explanation right now, but basically notice that your parameter estimates are really just getting rearranged. All your estimates are the same between the two models except for the last term. When you force lme() to exclude a main effect of soil, you're simply forcing the algebra to operate differently. In this case, soilS:pc.1 in model 2 equals pc.1 + soilS:pc.1 from model 1. Think of it this way: let's say you want the mean estimate for S soil and and a PC1 score of 2.3 (just made that up).

In model 1: (Intercept)  + soilS  + 2.3 * (pc.1  + soilS:pc.1)
In other words, you have to factor in the interaction term since you're considering the influence of PC1 in S soil. The interaction term is telling you how the effect of PC1 is modified if you're in S soil. So in order to get the total effect of PC1 in S soil you take the standard PC1 estimate (which applies to N soil) and modify it with the interaction term.
This equals: 1.9013061 + 2.2164100 + 2.3 * (-0.1470138 + 0.2734306)

In model 2: (Intercept)  + soilS  + 2.3 * (soilS:pc.1)
You forced the model to drop the default PC1 term, which just resulted in a re-factoring of the math.
This equals: 1.9013061 + 2.2164100 + 2.3 * (0.1264168)

So it's working out exactly the same.

I'm unclear what your exact goal is, but I'd be cautious about what you seem to be trying to do. Including an interaction without the main effect is likely to lead to a world of confusion. And if you're trying to estimate the effect of being in S soil, the effect of being in N soil, and the effect of PC1 within each of those soil types then you need exactly four parameters. Both of your models contain four parameters, in total have the exact same information, and address that question. You just asked the model to apportion out the algebra differently.

Hope that helps!
Evan
